analysis.one_liner: Requires independent audits and anti-discrimination rules for AI used in hiring, lending, housing, and other major decisions.
analysis.headline: The Artificial Intelligence Civil Rights Act was introduced in the House on December 2, 2025 with 30 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, and has had no committee action since it was referred to two committees.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to use an algorithm that discriminates by race, sex, age, disability, income, and other protected traits when the algorithm affects major life decisions — hiring, housing, credit, insurance, health care, government benefits, court and policing decisions, and elections. Companies would have to test high-risk algorithms with independent auditors before launch, publish audit summaries, let people opt out to a human decision-maker, and appeal to a human. Enforcement would come from the FTC, state attorneys general, and lawsuits by individuals, with penalties of at least $15,000 per violation and a ban on forced arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: People on the receiving end of automated decisions: job applicants and workers graded or screened by algorithms, renters and buyers facing algorithmic appraisals and lending, patients and insurance claimants, people whose benefits, ballots, or court outcomes are touched by automated systems, and workers who blow the whistle on flawed AI.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits using an algorithm in a way that causes a disparate impact or otherwise discriminates by race, color, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, disability, income, age, veteran status, and other protected traits in decisions about employment, education, housing, utilities, health care, credit, insurance, criminal justice, elections, and government benefits.

Requires a preliminary harm screening for every covered algorithm used in a consequential action, and a full independent-auditor evaluation before deployment when harm is plausible, covering the data used, testing across demographic groups, and the algorithm's potential for disparate impact.
Gives individuals a right to opt out of an algorithmic decision and have a human make it instead, and a right to appeal an algorithmic decision to a human, with rules to be set by the FTC.
Bans retaliation against people who exercise rights under the bill and protects whistleblowers who report violations.
Requires plain-language public disclosures, in the 10 most common US languages and accessible to people with disabilities, plus a public FTC repository of algorithm audits.

Lets individuals sue with treble damages or $15,000 per violation (whichever is greater), plus attorney's fees, invalidates pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the bill, and lets state attorneys general seek penalties of $15,000 per violation or 4 percent of a company's average gross annual revenue.
Authorizes the FTC to hire up to 500 additional staff and directs the Office of Personnel Management to create a federal occupational series for algorithm auditors.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that develop or deploy algorithms used in high-stakes decisions — from large AI labs to banks, insurers, landlords, employers, and government contractors using off-the-shelf tools — would bear audit fees, record-keeping for at least 10 years, disclosure obligations, and litigation and penalty exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: AI developers and companies deploying algorithms

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are substantial: developers and deployers must run preliminary screenings for every consequential use, engage independent auditors when harm is plausible, submit evaluations to the FTC within 30 days, keep records for at least 10 years, and publish disclosures in 10 languages.

The independent-auditor definition disqualifies anyone involved in developing or deploying the algorithm or holding a financial interest in the company, which could leave a thin pool of qualified auditors and concentrate a new mandatory audit market in a few firms.
Companies may redact trade secrets from published audit summaries, which limits how much the public can actually verify from the required disclosures and the FTC repository.

Critics of algorithm-audit mandates argue the cost and liability exposure could slow the deployment of beneficial automated tools, and the bill's broad definitions leave significant discretion to FTC rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — a legal right to a non-discriminatory process, a human alternative, an appeal, and real money damages — are large for individuals facing automated decisions in hiring, housing, credit, and benefits. The costs fall on the companies deploying these systems, though some of those costs would ultimately be passed to consumers, and small businesses using off-the-shelf AI tools face the same paperwork as large ones. The design leans on mandatory independent audits, which are a real safeguard but also create a new industry with a financial stake in the mandate it enforces.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Oversight committees on December 2, 2025, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-NY) introduced the bill on December 2, 2025 with 22 original cosponsors, and 29 Democratic cosponsors joined in total.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, with consideration to be determined by the Speaker.
No hearing, markup, or floor action has been recorded since the referral, and no Republican has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that develop or use algorithms in hiring, lending, housing, insurance, and other high-stakes decisions are better off so far, because no anti-discrimination or audit requirements have advanced, and the liability, audit costs, and private lawsuits the bill would create have not materialized. The newly emerging algorithm-auditing industry also gains nothing yet, since the mandatory audit market the bill would create has not been established.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.industry: AI developers and companies deploying algorithms in hiring, lending, housing, insurance, and government services
industries.note: The bill imposes mandatory harm screenings, independent audits, disclosures, a right to human decision-making, and private lawsuits with penalties of $15,000 or more per violation — costs and liability these companies do not currently face for algorithmic discrimination. The bill exists precisely because these systems currently shape hiring, credit, and housing without those checks.

The bill would create a mandatory market: any developer or deployer whose algorithm plausibly risks harm must hire an independent auditor, and it directs OPM to build a federal algorithm-auditing profession. The auditors' interest in a growing mandate runs alongside the public's interest in testing, though a too-small auditor pool could concentrate the market.

The bill makes the FTC the lead enforcer and authorizes up to 500 additional staff plus appropriations, expanding its jurisdiction over entities like banks, airlines, and common carriers that it otherwise cannot reach.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, referral to two committees, and no recorded committee action weeks after introduction, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote this Congress; the realistic path is that it sits in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, as most first-term civil rights and tech-regulation bills do. Its main practical value is as a draft for a future Congress or for state legislatures.
